title: Vicky Kaushal Has Blocked 18 Months of His Life for One Role. Bollywood Has Never Seen This Kind of Devotion.
excerpt: The actor will undergo a six-month physical transformation to play Parashurama in Amar Kaushik's mythological epic Mahavatar — and won't take a single other film until December 2027.
body:
There is a moment in every actor's career where they stop chasing box office numbers and start chasing legacy. For **Vicky Kaushal**, that moment is now.

The 38-year-old has quietly blocked an 18-month window — starting this month — exclusively for **Mahavatar**, Amar Kaushik's upcoming mythological epic about **Chiranjeevi Parashurama**, the sixth avatar of Lord Vishnu. No brand shoots squeezed in between setups. No quick cameos for friends. No parallel productions. Just one man, one character, and a year and a half of total, unbroken immersion.

In an industry that runs on multi-film calendars and back-to-back announcements, this is the kind of commitment Bollywood almost never sees.

## The Prep Alone Takes Six Months

Vicky is currently wrapping his work on **Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Love and War**, where he shares the screen with **Ranbir Kapoor** and **Alia Bhatt**. Bhansali is racing to complete a crucial 50-day schedule, with the film targeted for a January 21, 2027 theatrical release.

The moment Love and War wraps, Vicky switches gears entirely. A rigorous six-month preparation module begins — designed personally by director **Amar Kaushik** — that goes far beyond the gym. The transformation will require Vicky to bulk up into what insiders describe as a wrestler-like physique: heavy, rugged, with long matted hair and a presence that feels ancient and immovable.

> "Amar has designed a very detailed prep module for Vicky. It's not just about the physicality, but also about getting into the psychological and emotional graph of the character." — Source close to the production

This isn't just a diet plan and a new trainer. Kaushik has built an entire curriculum of acting workshops, character immersion sessions, and psychological deep-dives into the mythology of Parashurama — the Brahmin warrior who wielded an axe and is said to have rid the earth of corrupt kings twenty-one times over.

## Cameras Don't Roll Until January 2027

Principal photography is scheduled to begin in January 2027 and run for a full twelve months, with the production expected to wrap by December 2027. During this entire period, Vicky has made a conscious decision to take on zero other projects — a near-unprecedented move for an A-list Hindi film star at the peak of his commercial power.

> "Vicky is treating Mahavatar as a once-in-a-lifetime project. He wants to be fully invested, which is why he has consciously decided not to take up any other assignments during the shoot." — Pinkvilla

The scale of this commitment becomes clearer when you consider what Vicky is walking away from. After **Chhaava** (2025) delivered both critical praise and commercial success, and with Love and War promising to be one of 2027's biggest releases, Vicky could comfortably sign three or four films and stay in the conversation. Instead, he's choosing disappearance. He's choosing obsession.

## Amar Kaushik's Biggest Swing Yet

For director Amar Kaushik, Mahavatar represents a massive leap. The filmmaker behind **Stree** (2018), **Bhediya** (2022), and the blockbuster **Stree 2** (2024) has built his reputation on horror-comedies that blend Indian folklore with commercial entertainment. Mahavatar is something else entirely — a mythological epic that demands world-building on a scale Maddock Films has never attempted.

Producer **Dinesh Vijan** and the Maddock team have already begun extensive pre-production. The Director of Photography, along with art, production, and costume design teams, are deep into building the film's visual universe while Vicky transforms his body and mind.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs who grew up hearing stories of Parashurama at the dinner table or in Sunday morning *kathas*, Mahavatar could be the first time this particular avatar gets the theatrical treatment he deserves. The character occupies a fascinating space in Hindu mythology — a Brahmin who takes up arms, an immortal who walks the earth, a figure who embodies both devotion and destruction.

With Vicky's intensity, Kaushik's storytelling instincts, and Maddock's production muscle, this has the potential to be the kind of Indian mythological film that plays as well in Toronto and New Jersey as it does in Mumbai.

The film doesn't have a release date yet. But with a twelve-month shoot wrapping in late 2027, a 2028 release feels likely — which means the wait will be long. Then again, when an actor gives you eighteen months of his life for a single character, you probably owe him a little patience.
